title: What do common consulting and business terms mean, in plain English?
description: The business terms you will meet in case interviews, from ARPU to utilisation, each explained simply with an example.
hook: Most consulting jargon is a short name for a simple idea: churn is the share of customers who leave, contribution margin is what each sale adds after its own costs, and NPV is what future cash is worth today. Below, every term you are likely to meet in a case is explained in plain English, with why it matters and a worked example in dollars. The terms are grouped by topic so related ideas sit together.
body:
Revenue and customers

ARPU

Average revenue per user: revenue in a period divided by the number of customers. It is the "price" side of a subscription or telecom revenue tree, so when revenue falls, check whether it is fewer users or lower ARPU.

Example: $514M a year ÷ 12.6M subscribers ÷ 12 months ≈ $3.40 per subscriber per month.

ARR

Annual recurring revenue: the yearly value of all active subscriptions at a point in time. Used for software and other subscription businesses because it shows the revenue the company can expect if nothing changes.

Example: 2,000 customers paying $15,000 a year = $30M ARR.

CAC

Customer acquisition cost: sales and marketing spend divided by the number of new customers it brings in. On its own it means little; compare it with what a customer is worth (LTV).

Example: $900k of advertising ÷ 10,000 new customers = $90 per customer.

Churn

The share of customers who leave in a period. Average customer lifetime is roughly 1 ÷ churn rate, which is why small changes in churn move LTV a lot.

Example: 2% monthly churn means the average customer stays about 1 ÷ 0.02 = 50 months, and about 22% of customers leave over a year.

LTV

Lifetime value: the profit a customer brings over the whole time they stay. Monthly revenue × margin × expected months is the usual quick version. A healthy business earns well more from a customer than it spent to win them.

Example: $12 a month × 80% margin × 19 months ≈ $182. Against a $90 CAC, each customer is worth about 2× what they cost to acquire.

Net revenue retention

What last year's customers are worth this year, after cancellations, downgrades and upgrades, as a share of what they were worth before. Above 100% means existing customers are growing faster than others leave.

Example: A customer base worth $30M a year ago is now worth $27M: net revenue retention of 90%.

Market share

The client's sales as a share of the whole market. Always check the denominator: the right market, the right year, and units or value.

Example: $45M of sales in a $300M market = 15% share. If the market grows and sales do not, share falls.

Pricing power

The ability to raise prices without losing many customers, usually because of a strong brand, a product customers depend on, or little competition. It is the first thing to test before recommending a price rise.

Example: A software tool that firms rely on every day may be able to raise prices 5% a year with few cancellations.

Cannibalisation

When a new product or channel takes sales from your own existing ones instead of winning new customers. Only the sales that are genuinely new count towards the benefit of a launch.

Example: If 60% of a café's delivery orders replace a visit the customer would have made anyway, only 40% of delivery sales are new.

Switching costs

The money, time or hassle a customer faces to move to a rival. High switching costs keep customers loyal and make a market harder to enter.

Example: Moving a bank's core systems to a new vendor can take two years, so banks rarely switch.

Private label

A retailer's own-brand products, usually cheaper than branded ones and often more profitable for the retailer. A common threat in consumer goods cases.

Example: A supermarket's own cornflakes, sitting on the shelf next to the branded box.

Costs, margins and profit

Fixed and variable costs

Fixed costs do not change with volume in the short term (rent, head-office salaries). Variable costs rise with each unit made or sold (ingredients, delivery commissions). The split decides how profit reacts when volume changes.

Example: A restaurant's delivery-app commissions are variable; its lease is fixed.

Contribution margin

Price minus the variable cost of one unit: what each sale contributes towards fixed costs and profit. It is the number you need for break-even and for judging whether extra volume is worth having.

Example: A protein bar sells for $1.50 and costs $0.70 to make and ship: $0.80 contribution per bar.

Gross margin

Revenue minus the direct cost of the goods sold, as a share of revenue. It shows how much is left to pay for overheads and profit.

Example: $100M of sales with $60M cost of goods sold = $40M gross profit, a 40% gross margin.

Margin vs markup

Margin is profit as a share of price. Markup is profit as a share of cost. The same deal always has a higher markup than margin, and mixing them up is a classic case mistake.

Example: Cost $80, price $100: profit $20, so margin is 20% and markup is 25%.

Breakeven

The point (in units sold, or time) where revenue covers all costs, so profit is exactly zero. Break-even volume = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin per unit.

Example: $12M launch cost ÷ $0.80 contribution per bar = 15M bars to break even.

Operating leverage

How much profit swings when sales change. A business with mostly fixed costs has high operating leverage: a small rise in sales lifts profit a lot, and a small fall hurts a lot.

Example: An airline has $100M revenue, $15M variable costs and $75M fixed costs, so $10M profit. If revenue rises 10% to $110M, variable costs rise to $16.5M and profit becomes $18.5M: up 85%.

Utilisation

How much of available capacity is actually being used. Low utilisation means fixed costs are spread over too little output; very high utilisation means there is no room to grow without investing.

Example: 460M litres made in a 500M-litre plant = 92% utilisation.

Unit economics

Revenue and cost for a single unit of the business: one order, one customer, one store. If the unit does not make money, growing the business makes losses bigger.

Example: A delivery platform earns $9 commission on a $30 order, pays the rider $6 and spends $1.50 on payments and support: $1.50 contribution per order.

Capex and opex

Capex (capital expenditure) is spending on assets that last for years, such as a plant or equipment, paid upfront and used over their life. Opex (operating expenditure) is the ongoing cost of running the business, such as staff and rent.

Example: A $150M plant is capex; the staff, power and maintenance to run it each year are opex.

EBITDA

Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation: a rough measure of operating cash profit, widely used to compare and value companies. It is not the same as free cash flow, because capex, tax, interest and working capital still cost cash.

Example: A gym chain making $25M EBITDA, valued at 8× EBITDA, is worth about $200M.

Working capital

Cash tied up in running the business day to day: stock plus money customers owe you, minus money you owe suppliers. A growing business often needs more of it, which can squeeze cash even when profit looks healthy.

Example: $10M of stock + $15M owed by customers − $8M owed to suppliers = $17M of working capital.

Investment and valuation

Payback period

How long it takes for an investment to earn back what it cost. Quick and intuitive, but it ignores the time value of money and anything earned after payback.

Example: A $20M upgrade that adds $10M of profit a year pays back in 2 years.

NPV

Net present value: the value today of all future cash flows, minus the upfront cost. Positive NPV means the investment earns more than the cost of capital.

Example: −$1.5M upfront plus $153k a year for 25 years, discounted at 8%, gives an NPV of about +$133k, so it is worth doing, just.

DCF

Discounted cash flow: valuing a business or project by adding up its future cash flows, each reduced (discounted) to what it is worth today.

Example: At a 10% discount rate, $100 received in a year is worth $100 ÷ 1.1 ≈ $91 today, and $100 in two years is worth $100 ÷ 1.21 ≈ $83.

Cost of capital

The return investors expect for the risk they take, and so the discount rate for NPV. A project only creates value if it returns more than this.

Example: A project returning 8% destroys value if the cost of capital is 10%.

Perpetuity

The value today of a steady cash flow that goes on forever: cash flow ÷ discount rate. If the cash flow grows at a steady rate, divide by (discount rate − growth rate) instead.

Example: $5M a year at 8% is worth $62.5M. If it grows 3% a year, it is worth $5M ÷ 5% = $100M.

IRR

Internal rate of return: the yearly return an investment earns over its life, or the discount rate at which its NPV is zero. Private equity cases often give a target return of around 20% or more.

Example: Tripling your money in 6 years is an IRR of about 20% a year.

Money multiple

Cash a fund gets back divided by cash it put in. Also called MOIC (multiple on invested capital). Unlike IRR, it ignores how long the money was tied up.

Example: $40M in and $130M out is 3.25× the money. Over five years that is an IRR of about 27%.

Multiple

A quick way to value a business: a number times its profit or revenue, based on what similar companies are worth.

Example: 8× EBITDA of $25M = $200M.

Enterprise value (EV)

What the whole business is worth to all its funders: equity value plus net debt (debt minus cash). Multiples of EBITDA give enterprise value, not the value of the shares.

Example: Equity $245M + net debt $60M = EV $305M.

CAGR

Compound annual growth rate: the steady yearly growth that takes you from a start value to an end value. The rule of 72 gives a quick estimate: 72 ÷ years to double.

Example: A market that doubles from $50M to $100M in 7 years has a CAGR of about 10.4% (72 ÷ 7 ≈ 10.3%).

Opportunity cost

The value of the best alternative you give up by choosing something. In capacity and investment cases it is often the hidden cost that changes the answer.

Example: A factory line making housings cannot also make brackets worth $2.8M a year, so that $2.8M is a cost of the housings.

Deals and acquisitions

Due diligence

The checks a buyer does before an acquisition or investment: financial, commercial, legal and operational. In a case, it is what you would want to verify before recommending the deal.

Example: Testing whether a recycling company can really make the food-grade plastic it promises before paying for that capability.

Synergies

Extra value created by combining two businesses: cost savings or extra revenue neither could get alone. Cost synergies are usually more reliable than revenue synergies.

Example: Two distributors sharing warehouses and lorries save $5M a year.

Earn-out

Part of an acquisition price paid later, only if the business hits agreed targets. It bridges a gap between what the seller thinks the business is worth and what the buyer will risk.

Example: $160M upfront plus up to $20M more if premium contracts are signed within two years.

Case-solving terms

Hypothesis

Your best guess at the answer, stated early so you can test it with data and change it if the data disagrees. See hypothesis-driven thinking.

Example: "I suspect delivery costs are the issue, so I'd start there."

MECE

Mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive: buckets that do not overlap and together cover everything important. It is how interviewers judge a structure. See MECE explained.

Example: Revenue and costs are MECE for profit. "Marketing problems" and "customer problems" are not, because they overlap.

Terms that are easy to mix up

  • Revenue and cash. Revenue is the value of sales recorded; cash is what has actually been collected. A company can book sales while still waiting to be paid.
  • EBITDA and free cash flow. EBITDA leaves out capex, tax, interest and changes in working capital. A capital-hungry business can have strong EBITDA and weak cash.
  • Margin and markup. Same profit, different denominator: price for margin, cost for markup. More in margin vs markup.
  • Unit share and value share. Selling 1M units in a 10M-unit market is 10% unit share, but value share is higher if your products cost more than average.
  • IRR and money multiple. 2× in two years and 2× in ten years have the same multiple but very different IRRs.
  • Payback and NPV. Payback says how fast; NPV says how much value. Payback and NPV worked examples shows both on one case.

How to use these terms in an interview

Use a term only when it makes you clearer. "Each customer is worth about twice what we pay to win them" lands better than "LTV to CAC is 2×" if the interviewer has not used the jargon first. Whenever a metric appears, ask four questions: what exactly is counted, over what period, in what units, and divided by what? That habit turns vocabulary into analysis.

If an interviewer uses a term you do not know, ask. "Just to check, by utilisation do you mean hours billed over hours available?" sounds careful, not ignorant.
